speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EUROPEAN SITUATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the developments of the past week render it desirable that I should make a brief statement on the international situation. Many of the factors are not yet clear. When I come to take up the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, I shall seek to go fully into many questions which the happenings of last year and in particular, of the past few months, have created for Canada as for other countries.
I have been taken to task for some guarded references I made at the beginning of the month to the European situation. I pointed out on the first instant that a critical situation was still existing in the world, and that at some moment we might be called upon to consider questions larger than any we had thus far discussed. It will be realized now that these apprehensions had some foundation; so, I believe, had the feeling that the outlook was improving, to which I referred a week later. It will be observed that in stating on March 7th that I believed relief had been experienced in the foreign offices of Europe, that the situation had somewhat cleared in the few previous days, I was careful to add that I still adhered to what I had said on the previous occasion as something which, all the circumstances considered, it was proper I should have given to hon. members.
I made no claim to any exclusive sources of information, or to any ability to forecast the future. The form and place of the latest disturbance was a surprise to me, and a surprise to many governments more nearly concerned, and more minutely informed. I am

sure this house will always be desirous alike of facing unwelcome realities and of avoiding giving way to panic or propaganda. I have myself no desire either to ignore the serious shock the events of the past week have given to the world's hope of peace, or to exaggerate the imminence or extent of danger, as if the world were heading for Armageddon.
We have witnessed this past week the wanton and forcible occupation by Germany of the greater part of what remained of the Czecho-Slovak republic. Following this example, whether or not with Germany's approval, Hungary has occupied the remaining fragment, small, but racially and strategically important. After Munich, it was hoped that what remained of the Czecho-Slovak republic would be immune from aggression. That hope has not been realized. There are few countries which do not regret the fate which has now overtaken that gallant and vigorous small nation. They regret still more the evidence a great country has given that it does not consider itself bound by pledges freely exchanged a few short months before, and that it looks to force as the sole basis of relations with its neighbours, and apparently with the world. The occurrences of the week cannot find any defence, as may have appeared to be the case with some of the earlier manoeuvres, as reactions against excessive terms of the treaty of Versailles, or in the principles of self-determination and racial unity.
For the present at least, so far as we know, no country in all Europe is planning by counter force to reverse the result of force in Czechoslovakia. It is rather a question of weighing the results and considering what further moves may lie in the future. What is now needed is to take stock, as fully as may be possible, and to be ready for developments as they take actual shape out of the fog of conjectures; to prepare for all possible contingencies.
Mr. Chamberlain, in his frank and moving speech at Birmingham, asked, Was this the end of an old adventure, or the beginning of a new, the last attack on a small state, or the beginning of an attempt to dominate the world by force? He did not attempt to answer those questions, but declared they would require consideration not only by Germany's neighbours but by others even outside of Europe, and that the government of the United Kingdom would consider them in consultation with the members of the British commonwealth, France and various other powers.
So far as Canada is concerned, the government is ready at any time to take part in such consideration, to join in consultation

European Situation
with the United Kingdom and with such other countries as would be appropriate. I note that in speaking at Westminster to-day, Mr. Chamberlain told the House of Commons that Great Britain "requires to give full consideration" to the tense European situation in conjunction with other powers, "before any statement can be made." This wholly conforms with the statement made by Mr. Chamberlain at Birmingham on Friday last when he said:
I am not prepared to commit this country by new and unspecified commitments operating under conditions which cannot now be foreseen.
The first necessity for Canada, as well as for Great Britain, is to rsift rumour from fact, to examine whether the re is a probability of further drives, and if so in what direction, and in what form.
It is essential to clarify the actual issue that may arise. It is important to know what country or countries may be concerned, and whether it is a case of agitation and propaganda, or of economic pressure, or of military force. It is equally important to know exactly what policies are being suggested to meet the situation, and what measure of support and feasibility those policies are likely to receive. With this knowledge the Canadian government will have little difficulty in proposing to this parliament any action which it believes should be taken in the contingency anticipated.
If there were a prospect of an aggressor launching an attack on Britain, with bombers raining death on London, I have no doubt what the decision of the Canadian people and parliament would be. We would regard it as an act of aggression, menacing freedom in all parts of the British commonwealth. If it were a case, on the other hand, of a dispute over trade or prestige in some far corner of the world, that would raise quite different considerations.
Canada at all times has been prepared to consult, as occasion might arise, with other freedom loving countries as to the most effective means of cooperation against aggression. The form of such cooperation and the contingency in which it may arise, are questions which this government will examine, in consultation with other governments. It will report its findings and any proposals that may result to this parliament, which has the sole and responsible authority to speak for Canada in such grave issues. I still believe in parliament as the most important of our national institutions; and in the supremacy of parliament, especially where the issue is one of peace or war. I may add that, as would be expected in the circumstances, no statement of the policy the United Kingdom government has in mind has yet been received, from London.
In spite of the shock to the world's confidence, there is no reason to despair of peace, or to cease working for peace. The world has come to be able to stand shocks, to make readjustments which a few years ago would have made open conflict inevitable.
The peoples of the different countries of the world do not want war. No government of any democratic country has any thought or intent of making war. No government of any totalitarian country can hope for passive acquiescence in acts of international lawlessness, as they come to effect a wider range of powers, nor can they anticipate victory over the limitless moral and material resources that would be arrayed against them. It is a time for preparedness, but equally for furthering to the utmost, conciliation and cooperative effort among all peoples.
I think I may say with no less sincerity than Mr. Chamberlain that there is scarcely anything I would not sacrifice for peace, but, like Mr. Chamberlain, there is one thing I must except, and that is the liberty which we enjoy and which we will never surrender. I believe this is the feeling of every Canadian who loves his country and cherishes its liberties. Acts of aggression and attempts at world domination by force are just as hateful to the people of Canada as they are to the peoples of the United Kingdom, the United States, France and all other peace loving and freedom loving democracies.

subtopic: EUROPEAN SITUATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I make it very clear to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that I have never yet attempted to speak for his party, and I do not expect I ever shall do so. I know he is quite capable of speaking for them himself. I was not intending to speak for anyone but the National Conservative party, of which I have the honour to be the head.
I listened with very great interest to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I do not intend to discuss it in any way. I know the great difficulties of government in times like these, and it is certainly far from any thought in my mind to add in any way to those difficulties. Therefore, I shall offer no criticism and no jarring note of any kind. If there is anything that I think those in all sections of the house and in all sections of this country should remember, it is that in a time like this we should be a united people, that we should do everything we can to hold this nation together. I have never been able to see what good would be done to the empire if this country were split down the middle and divided again into the various parts that existed before confederation. I certainly believe in being tolerant of everyone's opinion, whether or not it agrees with my own.
I consider this whole question as being too serious for political manoeuvring of any kind. It should be above and beyond anything in the way of playing politics, anything in the way of attempting to gain some petty political advantage or anything of that sort. In every statement I have made I have endeavoured to show that I want to be as helpful as I can.
It seems to me that even more is at stake to-day than was at stake in September last. At that time only a fringe of Czecho-Slovakia, the Sudetenland, was at stake. To-day it strikes me that all the personal liberties and

European Situation
parliamentary institutions of democracy are at stake. In a sense, it is democracy and Christianity against Hitler's totalitarianism. That is the way it strikes me, at any rate. On numerous occasions Hitler has shown his antagonism to Christianity. I was startled to read yesterday that the Protestant leader Niemoller was still in a concentration camp. I thought he had been let out some time ago. He has been in that camp for nearly two years. Both Catholics and Protestants have been attacked by Hitler. Therefore, I look upon this whole question as being something very much above ordinary affairs. All our liberties are at stake, and I repeat that so far as I am concerned I am ready to help in every possible way. I will do nothing to muddy the waters and confuse the issues, or to hinder the actions of the government.
I agree with the Prime Minister that the whole world has been shocked at what has taken place. I would use much stronger language than he. Perhaps I am prone to use much stronger language than the Prime Minister. I say that this attack of Hitler's on Czecho-Slovakia, this taking over of Czechoslovakia, was unprovoked, unlawful and brutal. As Mr. Chamberlain pointed out, it was a violation of Hitler's word and agreement. No doubt all hon. members have read of how the secret police have taken over in this little freedom-loving country. Until recently Czecho-Slovakia had as its head one of the most outstanding statesmen of Europe, Doctor Bernes. I had the honour of meeting him and knowing him fairly well at the meetings of the League of Nations, where the representatives of Great Britain, France and many other prominent countries used to consult with him on vital questions. This country, which had been governed by one of the most broadminded, statesmanlike gentlemen, has been overrun with secret police. The people are being told they must not stay out after nine o'clock at night and that they must have nothing in the way of assembly. I was shocked, and the peoples of all freedom-loving countries of the world must have been shocked at such news as that.
I turn now to Mr. Chamberlain's language. I should like to refer briefly to what he said at Birmingham. It must be remembered that when Mr. Chamberlain uses strong language it is really much stronger than when the same language is used by the ordinary citizen. Mr. Chamberlain has always been known for his moderation, his toleration and his gentle humility. The Prime Minister probably knows him very well, and some of us on this side came to know him intimately when he was over here at the empire conference of 1932.
I have put it on record publicly that I consider him the outstanding British representative at the conference, and the most gentle and considerate of men. The fact that he used the language he did at Birmingham shows how he was shocked at this brutal and barbarous attack of Hitler upon Czechoslovakia.	Mr. Chamberlain asked what
reliance could be put upon the word of Hitler. I am putting this in my own language. He said that Czecho-Slovakia had been wantonly attacked. That word " wanton " is very strong language. He said that Germany would bitterly regret the attitude which her leader had taken. This is the language of a man who, with the possible exception of the former Pope, has been the greatest peacemaker in the world. Pope Pius XI was noted as one of the greatest peacemakers the world has ever had. Mr. Chamberlain is a man who hates war from the bottom of his soul, as he has publicly stated over and over again. He is a man who believes above all in the council table in preference to the battlefield. He believes in the Kellogg-Briand pact; in the settling of international disputes by conciliation rather than by war. This is the man who humbled himself by going to Berchtesgaden, to Godesberg and to Munich, and when he used such strong language he must have been outraged to a terrific extent. I did not hear him over the radio, but I am told by those who did that his language was more severe than would appear from the press reports.
These conquerors moved into Czechoslovakia, a freedom-loving country in the truest sense of the word. We see the Jews who have been living peacefully in that country immediately persecuted. Such action is shocking to all of us. It is shocking to the whole world to see Jews or any other people maltreated in this way.
Mr. Sumner Welles, with the approval of President Roosevelt, has referred to this display of wanton force. His language is even stronger than that used by Mr. Chamberlain. Mr. Welles referred to "acts of wanton lawlessness and arbitrary force." He also used the language "threatening world peace and the very structure of modem civilization." We ask ourselves, in view of that strong language, what must we expect next from this madman? To my mind this man is very close to a madman. He is at least acting like one, and no one knows what we may expect next, least of all Hitler himself. He has a passion for world domination. He is mad with the lust for conquest, and he is aiming at absolute world domination.
European Situation

Now, sir, this is what I am going to suggest without taking up much more of the time of the house: I think that this above all times is the time when all Canadians should stand unitedly together and should make -it clear that all democratic countries stand in a solid front against the international criminality-because that is what it is-that Hitler is attempting to impose upon the world. He broke the terms of the treaty of Versailles. He fortified the Rhineland. He marched into Austria and took possession of it. He took over the Sudeten territory of Czecho-Slovakia practically by force, and now without any justification he takes over the whole of Czechoslovakia. I say it is time for the democracies of the world, for the United Kingdom and the dominions, France, the United States, the smaller free nations, and all others throughout the world who want to stop this mad ambition of Hitler's, to stand together and make it clear that they are standing together, morally at any rate.
I am not talking war, but it seems to me that the only way we can stop war is to show that there is a solid front amongst all the democratic, civilized, Christian peoples of the world against the attempts of this man to dominate the whole world.
There are people who say that war is inevitable, and I have had that said to me by outstanding people, but I do not believe that war is ever inevitable. As Earl Baldwin said at the time of the September crisis, if there is only a five per cent chance in favour of peace, I am in favour of peace. I believe in the democratic peoples of the world presenting a united front, not only the ones I have named but others who wish to join to bring this man Hitler to his senses. Such a solid front might possibly halt his mad career- might act as a "Stop; look, and listen" sign to him.
May I make it clear to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house and country that I am a strong peace lover. I am just as much in favour of peace as Mr. Chamberlain, or the Prime Minister or any other member of this house could possibly be. I am a peace lover from the bottom of my soul. I did have the opportunity to see, if I may be forgiven for mentioning it, the cruelties and horrors of war at first hand. I saw strong, young, healthy men turned through shell shock into nervous wrecks, crying for help; I saw mutilations and blindness; and we all know that sixty thousand of our best young Canadians lie in Europe. We all know the failure of the great war into which the world was plunged by the man who preceded Hitler
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
in Germany, the kaiser, who was not as dangerous a man as Hitler. And yet to-day because of dictatorships, particularly the German dictatorship, armaments are greater than ever before. We know what war involves, and those of us who happen to have served are the most antagonistic to war. I think there is no body of people in all Canada so antagonistic to war as the four or five hundred thousand returned men in this country. They are the strongest of all for peace. We saw that the last war, which was to make the world safe for democracy, did not do so. Democracy is in a more precarious position to-day than it has ever been. The war to end war, as it was supposed to have been, failed to end war. Our ideals have been shattered.
On top of all that knowledge, I have three boys of my own. I am a father who loves his children and does not want to see them used for cannon fodder. I sympathize with all fathers and mothers, and so I say that I have every reason in the world to hate war from the bottom of my soul. But we must remember the self-preservation, not only of our own country, but of all democratic nations. The whole aim of my remarks to-day is not to say what we must do in war; my aim is to prevent war if at all possible, and I say that all the democracies of the world, all the peace loving nations, should stand together at this time in a stern moral protest against this man Hitler and his attempt to dominate the world. We must show a united front, and show it frankly and courageously, and if we all do that there will probably be no war. That, sir, is the prayer of us all.
As leader of the National Conservative party I offer now to join loyally and wholeheartedly with the government in making it clear to all the world that a united Canadian people-with one mind and one heart-is determined, come what may, to preserve its liberties and its nationhood. And may God assist us in our efforts!

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: EUROPEAN SITUATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I 'have no prepared statement. As I said a few moments ago, it does not seem to me perhaps quite proper that we should delay at any length now to deal with the entire European situation.
I would say, however, dealing with what was said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), that if we had been morally united the world would not have been in the fix in which it finds itself to-day. We can-

European Situation
not, look back to the treaty of Versailles, -the treaty of the victors-and to the history of the past fifteen years without realizing that there has been a series of blunders. We did not take seriously the principles underlying the League of Nations.
I would say that at this critical time we should utilize as far as may be the existing machinery of collective peace action. There is an enormous power in the united peace action of the leading nations of the world. Although we have heard it said that the league is practically defunct, there is yet sufficient vitality in the league, if we rally around it, to do something before it is too late. Also, although the United States is outside the league, their people are very much the same as ours in sentiment, and every effort should be made to establish the very closest cooperation with the United States.
At this time I would offer three simple practical suggestions as to what we in Canada might do. First of all, it is high time that there should be an immediate prohibition of the export of war materials to Germany. That is something practical. It is something that might interfere with the profits of some of our Canadians; in my judgment we should have done it long ago, but. I urge upon the government, since it has not been done in the past, that we at once prohibit the export of war materials to Germany and to any other aggressor nation.

speechtext: I have no prepared speech at all, but perhaps a few words are in order. Certain it is that this is the time for unity; for unity politically, racially and socially. This ought to be a time not only for talking about unity but for seeking out and adopting and applying such policies as will remove the causes of disunity. I long for peace; I believe that war results from ignorance and the application of mistaken policies. Both ignorance and false policies can be removed. It is our solemn duty at this hour of great peril, first, to stand together within our own country; second, to take counsel earnestly with our neighbours; finally to seek out, discover and remove the mistaken policies and the ignorance which are driving us blindly towards war.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I heard with great interest the remarks made the other night by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). While I cannot go all the way with him in his pronounced views with regard to free trade, I appreciated greatly the case he outlined. While I do not believe in high tariff, I have had occasion too often to advocate in this house protection for some industry or interest in my district to take an attitude entirely against it. I prefer to deal with each case as it arises.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw was able to make out a strong case for free trade as against protection owing to the surrounding circumstances in connection with the matter to which he was alluding. In one respect the case is even. worse than he represented it to be. On page 2015 of Hansard he said, speaking of the repeal of the duty on Japanese oranges:
Although the dictionary said that a Japanese orange was an orange, although the trade always called the Japanese orange an orange, an order in council was passed at that time, saying that a loose-skinned mandarin or tangerine was not an orange and therefore could enter Canada free. But other oranges, the same tangerines and mandarins from the United States, were still subject to the same duty of 35 cents per cubic foot.
The hon. member has fallen into the same error that I did. I fully thought that those were the circumstances, that the duty was put on against oranges. Then it was discovered by a strained construction of the meaning of the word "oranges" that a tangerine was, botanically speaking, not an orange, and therefore was not liable to the duty. If that had been the case the matter would have been adjusted by a mere ruling of the Minister of National Revenue. But it was not done in that way. It was done by order in council, P.C. 2980, which I shall read, as it is only a few lines:
At the Government House at Ottawa Monday, the 30th day of November, 1931.
Present:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister

of National Revenue and under the powers granted by section 11 of the customs tariff to make such reductions of duties on goods imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for reductions on Canadian products granted by any such country or countries, and under any other power thereunto enabling, is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered that mandarins and tangerines, when grown in Japan and imported into Canada direct from that country, be admitted free of customs duty.
sgd. "E. J. Lemaire,"
Clerk of the Privy Council.
So the house will see that they were allowed to come in not because it was held that they were not oranges, in which case the exemption would have applied also to tangerines and mandarins of all countries; but it was confined entirely to tangerines and mandarins when grown in Japan. The order in council says that it was done under a section of the Customs Act which allows a reduction of duty when a similar reduction is made by another country. There was no similar reduction made in this instance, and therefore it was done under the words cited, "and under any other power thereunto enabling;" for it is on record that there was no reduction made by Japan in that regard or in any other regard calling for compensating action on our part. Therefore we were put in the unique position that we had pledged ourselves to give free entry and preference to oranges from the British empire, particularly Africa and Australia, and for that reason we put a duty against all foreign oranges, of which we imported large numbers. That was in May, 1931, and in November of the same year, before the duty had any effect on importations from Japan, the government of that day passed an order in council providing that if the tangerines were grown in Japan, and in Japan only, they would come in free of duty. I think the circumstances call for an explanation from somebody as to why that took place. The result was that we continued to buy our oranges from California and Japan principally, and we either paid a higher price or got an inferior orange. People who could not afford to buy oranges above a certain grade took an inferior grade.
I had some communication with an official recently about the matter. I shall not give his name because it might be supposed that I am criticising him, and I am not. He is a man of great ability, of the greatest courtesy, and went to no end of trouble to give me the information I wanted. Here is a phrase he used in connection with this matter which struck me, to use the vernacular, right in

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the eye. Speaking of putting Japan and Australia on the same basis in this matter, he writes:
Undoubtedly cancellation of the order in council would be resented by the Japanese government, a fact which would have to be given consideration by the government of Canada.
Surely we have not come to the situation in this day and generation that we cannot put on a small duty or a large one against the products of another country without its being resented by that country. But if that is so, it is time we knew where we are heading for.
When the Minister of Finance presents his budget, so to speak, the Canadian tariff, and is making adjustments, as I suppose he will, I hope that he will take occasion to adjust the matter I have referred to which was dealt with by order in council and impose a duty on mandarins and tangerines of Japanese origin as is done on mandarins and tangerines from any other country in the world.

Under the new agreement the date of application of the duty on oranges has been changed to the first of December, as compared with the first of January under the old agreement. If any change is to be made it should be the other way. The duty on oranges should extend over a longer period than it does at the present time. As an apple grower I feel that taking the duty off oranges would be detrimental to the apple growers and apple shippers of this country. We heard a good deal on Friday from the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) about the advantage of having cheap oranges in this country, but I have a letter here from an apple shipper and an apple grower in which he says:
You are quite moderate in your remarks about the competition of oranges. Your own Spy apples will give you an example. Mine is worse. In December I sent a car of choice Baldwins to the terminal market in Montreal and it arrived the week before Christmas, when forty-one carloads of oranges came in from the United States. Apples at once took a giant tumble and I lost over $1.50 a barrel over preceding prices. You will agree that that is a big tax to pay against my production. While I was there, a New York firm telegraphed the agents offering to send in other carloads of oranges at $1.88 a box f.o.b. Montreal.
I took the trouble to call up a fruit distributing house in Ottawa before I came down to the house and he tells me that 288 oranges to a case is the popular-sized orange. That costs the wholesaler S2.50 a case, which is less than one cent apiece. I contend that no apple grower in Ontario or British Columbia or anywhere else in this country 71492-1291
can grow apples and compete with oranges sold at less than one cent apiece. I also contend that as far as the consumer is concerned, that is not a reasonable price. Even if the consumer were paying two cents apiece it would still be a cheap article of food. There is really no comparison at all between an orange and an apple. While some say there are more vitamins in an orange, some say there are more salts. I should like to see the time extended to January 1 instead of December 1. If you turn the page you will see that this is permissible. It would not at all satisfy me-for as an apple grower I contend it should be March 1 before oranges come into this country free,-but if nothing can be done about that we have to accept the agreements as they are. I believe I voice the sentiments of the apple growers of Ontario when I say they are certainly not satisfied with this. I hope the government will try to do something which will give the apple growers of Canada a fair deal.

The two main countries that were to be protected were Australia and South Africa. Australia grows only 2,500,000 cases of oranges all told, and Canada eats that much in an ordinary year. South Africa grows only 3,000,000 cases a year, and during this last year, 1938, according to the returns as brought down for the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) not one case of oranges came from Australia and only 130 cases came from South Africa.
The other evening I made the statement that the oranges which were allowed in free during January, February, March and April did not necessarily come from California. The hon. member for Kootenay East said the flush production of oranges in California was from December to April. I disagreed with my hon. friend; I said he was entirely wrong, and he maintained he was not. I stated that in California navel oranges are ripened, picked and shipped during November, December and January, and Valencia oranges during April, May, June and July. The hon. member for Kootenay East questioned my statement and said that there was a much smaller quantity of Valencias than of navels; according to him the quantity of Valencias was of small importance. As Minister of Trade and Commerce at the time the treaty was made he exhibited about the same amount of knowledge concerning this business as he did the other evening in the house. As a matter of fact in the part of California, of which he was speaking, there are some 94,000 acres all told producing navel oranges, which are packed during the months I stated^ and 145,000 acres producing Valencia oranges, which the hon. member said were the smaller amount. It would be well for anyone when speaking in this house to try to have the facts and to give only the facts.
In connection with this item, according to the trade treaty, there is a different period which might be used. I would say that Australia is not affected by importations of oranges in December, but might be affected by oranges imported in July, provided they shipped oranges to Canada, which they have not done for the last year. But Canada is a large country. Oranges that enter at the

Therefore, a treaty that takes in these months may make a difference to the eastern shippers, that is the British West Indies, or South Africa, and no difference to the western shippers. In other words, it does not matter whether you have the month of July free in the east to the British West Indies r South Africa, nor does it matter whether mu have the month of December free in the *rest so far as Australia is concerned; but the tremendous cost to the consumers of Canada should be taken into account.
But something else should also be noted. As I said the other night, this is just an instance of what was done to the people of Canada by the British empire agreements. We therein bound duties against decrease, and when you bind a duty against decrease you give to someone else the right to use the bargaining power of your tariff. This has been done in this and many other instances under the British empire agreements. In other words, we have placed our tariff where we cannot lower it in order to get concessions from another country when making a irade agreement with them. But it is quite conceivable that other countries within the British empire can use the right they have to allow us to lower that tariff in order to get concessions for themselves in trade treaties with other countries of the world. That is the worst feature that has ever been put in any trade agreement in Canada.
The trade treaty of 1932 was full of such items. There were 200 of these items, though there are now less than ninety. But when they were put there due consideration was not given to the cost, because in many instances, just as in connection with oranges, the British empire could not possibly supply from within the empire those commodities which we needed, and the net result was that there was a great rise in cost to the people of Canada for all the goods they had to buy under that treaty.

The hon. member, before being so caustic in his observations regarding myself, might have taken the trouble to look up the reasons that were advanced at the time this duty was imposed in 1932. Had he done so he would have found a few facts such as those that I shall mention in the course of a brief statement.
There was no suggestion that we should . impose this duty on oranges merely for the protection of oranges coming from Australia and South Africa. The point in the whole business was this. Some fifteen or twenty years ago Canada used to bring in oranges from the West Indies and from central American points as well as from other countries in competition with oranges from Florida, California and other parts of the United States. The competition at that time was exceedingly keen and the Canadian purchaser of oranges got all the advantages of a competitive market. During that period, twenty or twenty-five years prior to the imposition of the tariff in 1932, the citrus fruit growers of California attained such a high degree of exclusiveness of organization that they drove the West Indian orange growers out of this market, which was their best. Indeed, the West Indian growers were affected to such an extent that they uprooted their orchards as a complete loss in consequence of their having been denied the Canadian market.
Figures were given demonstrating this. The result was that oranges ceased to come in from the West Indies in competition with oranges from California, with the highly organized method of production there, and in consequence prices of oranges were higher during all subsequent years than they had been before. There was no competition; there was no competitive buying; the price was fixed by the citrus growers of California, who are recognized as the most highly organized and the most closely controlled industry in the United States. They seriously affected

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the production of oranges in Florida, which had also been a source of supply for the United States and Canada.
Having that situation in mind, recognizing that Canada has an excellent market in the West Indies for some of our products, and that there were few products that the West Indies could ship to Canada, we decided to impose this duty, which was really tantamount to a duty against California, upon the importation of oranges from the United States, in the hope and expectation that the West Indies would thereby be encouraged to replant their orange groves and restore the balance of competitive trade with the highly organized industry of California. Briefly, that is the story.
It is true that at the same time we hoped that we might develop some importations from Australia and South Africa, and we did. We brought in quite a number of shipments. The hon. member has quoted certain figures, but they relate to a condition which is subsequent to the change made in the tariff in the 1935-36 agreement. I say 1935-36, because the agreement came into effect on January 1, 1936. Prior to that time the rate was thirty-five cents a cubic foot the year round, and it was then amended, being free, for the months of January to April, but otherwise thirty-five cents a cubic foot. I have not the statistics before me, but I venture to say they will show there was considerable importation of oranges during those years prior to 1936; and had we maintained a tariff at that standard to give time for the development of the trade, we should undoubtedly have restored that very happy condition of external competition which we had aimed at in the imposition of this duty.
The hon. member takes an extravagant method of showing the effect of protection. He takes the total revenue collected on the importation of oranges from the United States and divides it by the importations from empire countries since the trade agreement of 1935. Then, by this method of arithmetical calculation, he says we are giving a protection of $40, $50, $60, $70, and I think it went up to $700 in one instance, per case to empire growers. Of course the argument is ludicrous and absurd in the extreme. It is an old trick in oratory and rhetoric to carry a thing to an absurd point in order to invite attention to the argument being presented.

speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations on this bill. I realize that a great deal of valuable work has been done under this act; nevertheless because of its limitations I think it is unable to deal adequately with the problems of the permanent drought area, and in referring to that area I have in mind that part of Alberta east of a line drawn north and south of the town of Hanna. In that area, in order to deal with the problem in such a way that a farmer might be able to enjoy a reasonable standard of living, I believe we are still faced with one of two alternatives, either to .make a greatly increased acreage of land available to the farmer in order that he may go into ranching, or to develop irrigation projects.
The first of these alternatives has been undertaken to a certain extent already by the special areas board of Alberta. For instance, in the Berry Creek area the aim has been to allow three thousand acres per family, with a definite limitation upon the amount of stock that can be carried per quarter section. I believe the limit is three head per quarter section or one head per fifty acres, because it is realized that in that area it takes about fifty acres of land to maintain one head of stock. Under this act a great deal of crested wheat grass seed has been distributed, and once that is established no doubt the number of head of stock per quarter section may be increased. Farmers, however, have been greatly handicapped by lack of finances with which to buy stock to build up their herds. This is especially so, following the unfortunate occurrence of a year ago when, owing to lack of feed, the federal government in conjunction with the provinces framed certain regulations under which the farmers were forced to reduce their stock in order to obtain relief feed. Now they find themselves in the unfortunate position of not having the money with which to 'buy stock to build up their
herds. So, as I have already stated, I believe a great deal of the drought area in Alberta- and possibly this applies to Saskatchewan as well-eventually will have to be turned back to grazing unless large irrigation projects are instituted.
A certain amount of the land in the drought area of Alberta is especially suitable for irrigation purposes. Many schemes have been surveyed and endorsed by engineers. Perhaps the best known scheme is the North Saskatchewan project, generally referred to as the William Pearce project. Under that scheme a million and a half acres would be irrigated, one million in Saskatchewan and half a million in Alberta. When the estimates were first prepared I think the cost was figured to be approximately S70 an acre to irrigate land in Saskatchewan; but according to certain well known engineers that figure can be considerably reduced to-day. I think it is estimated that it can be cut approximately in half. While the major project may be considered too expensive or not feasible, there are a number of modified schemes based upon the William Pearce project, such as, for instance, the Sullivan Lake project. Under that scheme half a million acres in Alberta would be irrigated, at a cost of approximately S23,000,000. In this instance also this figure probably could be cut considerably, on account of the fact that dirt can be moved very much more cheaply to-day than was the case when the original survey was made, and the further fact that at the present time this land is largely owned by the government, so there would be no necessity for buying very much land. These projects, however, are entirely beyond the financial resources of the province, and if they are to be put into operation they will have to be financed by the federal government. At the present time, as I understand it, this act is not so constituted that large irrigation projects can be financed, but I am hoping that, as time goes on, a change may be made which would allow these larger projects to be carried on.
If these schemes are put into operation without building up excessive charges against the land, I think they may become highly satisfactory, judging from past history. In Alberta to-day many of the larger irrigation projects are operating successfully; the farm-era are making a fairly decent living and are able to pay the maintenance costs. It is useless, however, to expect a project of this kind to be able to repay the capital charges, and if irrigation projects are to be put into operation in the future with any hope of success, we shall have to construct them without placing a charge against the land.

I should now like to say just a few words with regard to the methods of administration adopted under this act, because I do feel that in some ways the administration of this act in Alberta has been somewhat unfortunate. In my province there is a definite feeling that in the matter of expenditures there has been a great deal of discrimination against Alberta compared with Saskatchewan. Of course I realize that the area in Saskatchewan is very much larger than the area in Alberta, and this may partly account for this feeling. Apart from that, however, there are other reasons why people feel that Alberta has been discriminated against. I might mention one instance, the Bartman dam which was built in my constituency. The contract for this dam was awarded the Poole Construction Company, with headquarters in Regina, which put in a tender amounting to something like $19,332. The special areas board of Alberta put in a tender totalling about $150 less.

If it had been awarded to the special areas board, the work would have started far earlier than it did. The Poole Construction Company had to bring in their material and their outfit; a great deal of time was wasted, with the result that the spillway of the dam was not completed in time. When spring came, the water, instead of running down the spillway, ran over the top, and the dam was washed out. If that dam had been constructed ,by the special areas board, I believe this would not have happened, because only six miles below the Bartman dam the special areas board built what is known as the Helmer dam. Not only did that dam withstand the natural flow of water, it also withstood the force of the water which broke down the Bartman dam. Of course the Helmer dam is a smaller dam; nevertheless it was saved. Moreover, if that contract had been awarded to the special areas board, far more of the money would have been spent locally instead of going out of the district, as it did when it was paid to the Poole Construction Company. That, I think, was unnecessary. I suppose there was some reason for awarding that contract to this company, 
but their tender was higher than that of the special areas board, which was on the spot and which possessed a great deal of experience in building dams of this kind. So I think it was strange that the special areas -board did not obtain the contract.
Now that we are in committee I should like to ask the minister if he could give us any information as to whether or not any action is being taken along the line of investigating the Sullivan Lake project, and also whether any action is being contemplated or taken regarding the extension of the Medicine Hat irrigation -project. The minister knows the project to which I am referring; it is the one concerning which he was interviewed by a committee last month.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is possible for me to cover all the matters referred to by the hon. member, but perhaps I can recall most of his references and can deal with them pretty much in the order in which they were mentioned.
In the first place I quite agree it has been found necessary bo change the situation which had existed prior to 1932 in that section of the country lying east of Hanna in Alberta. At that time most of that territory was occupied by homesteaders, or persons who had homesteaded land and purchased preemptions. Since that time much of the area has been evacuated by those who originally settled it. Much of the land is light. It is not very well suited to grain growing of any kind, and is probably best suited to the production of live stock. However, the reference which was made a few minutes ago to the effect that it requires fifty acres of land to maintain one head of live stock indicates that it is not really very good live stock land. When an eastern farmer hears one referring to the fact that fifty acres of land are required to pasture one head of live stock, I am sure he wonders just what kind of country it is. That in itself indicates that it is not very productive, even of grass.
Therefore there were problems there when practically the whole of that country was settled by homesteaders. That was one of the mistakes which was made in settling the area in the first place. The Pearce scheme, which has been spoken of as a means of taking care of some of the difficulties which exist in the area from Hanna eastward to Saskatoon, is a scheme which has been discussed widely in both eastern and western Canada. I recall having seen about two years ago in some of the eastern papers strongly written editorials and news items to the effect that this was one more instance where the government was not taking the action it should take because this

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
scheme was not being put under way. I may add that some of the same papers to-day are accusing the government of spending too great sums of money in trying to deal with some of the problems we are attempting to deal with in connection with that area.
The Pearce scheme is one which was outlined many years ago by a gentleman named Pearce who had made explorations across that country. It necessitated first the filling of a storage known as Sullivan lake just to the north and a little to the west of Hanna, Alberta, and making use of that for the irrigation of about 425,000 acres of land in the immediate vicinity of Sullivan Lake. The idea was then to carry the waters farther down into Saskatchewan, using the storages at Tramping lake, and elsewhere between there and Saskatoon, to irrigate certain areas of land. I might point out that if the scheme had been undertaken and completed, there could have been irrigated in the whole section of the country only about a million and a half acres, as indicated by the hon. member a moment ago, whereas in that section of the country we are talking about there are probably 30,000,000 acres of land occupied by settlers. So that one can see that if one were going to irrigate only about a million and a half acres in an area where probably 30,000,000 acres are occupied by farmers, even the considerable expenditure of money that is talked about is not going to help many of them.
I believe much of the land which would have been brought under irrigation by the original scheme has since been found not to be very well suited to irrigation. Some of it is too light, and therefore permits the water to get away before it is of much use. Then, some of it is more or less affected by alkali which makes it difficult to irrigate to advantage. But a considerable part of the land could be irrigated, and about 425,000 acres of it is in the vicinity of Hanna and Sullivan Lake.
I have been asked whether anything is being done to explore the possibilities of the scheme, and I can say only that we have engineers on the job making investigations with regard to costs and possibilities in connection with the development of a storage in Sullivan lake. I understand it would be necessary first to build a dam in the river near Red Deer; after the dam was built, it would be necessary to pump the water up to the prairie level, which is an extremely expensive undertaking; then run it in ditches from that point until it reaches the river at another point; then syphon it under the river, bring
it up to the river again on the other side, take it down to Sullivan lake and fill that lake, making it a storage which can be used for irrigation purposes round Sullivan lake.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
I understand, if a dam
were built just below the mouth of the Raven river, on the Red Deer river, it would need to be only fifty feet high, and then the water would come down by gravity, without any pumping.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
If you build a dam
fifty feet high, take the water out of the river and run it down by gravity, it takes the water down along the river banks. I understand the nature of the soil is such that it will not hold water running in ditches along the level. In all probability you would find most of the water running back into the river before you got down to Sullivan lake.
The only practical scheme is one of pumping the water up to the level, taking it in ditches and then taking it back into Sullivan lake. That is an expensive undertaking and one which at the moment the department would not feel like recommending to the government. It is not an undertaking the department would recommend at the present time to the consideration of the house, as one which, with the amount of money available and the amount the house is prepared to vote for that kind of undertaking, we might want to undertake.
There are many other undertakings of a similar nature which, taken together, will, I believe, take care of more people with the expenditure of the same amount of money. But the investigations are not yet completed. The final report is not yet in, and I am only giving to the committee the benefit of the information which at present is before the department in relation to that particular project. I might say that one can quite understand what the expenditure would be in order to irrigate about a million acres in addition to this half million, when water has to be moved hundreds of miles from that location in order to have it where the additional land is to be irrigated.
Something has been said about its costing just about half as much to move earth now as it did some years ago. Well, I have had something to do with moving earth in Saskatchewan since about 1922, when I was minister of highways in that province. I find it costs just about as much to move earth today, even with more efficient machinery, as it did back in 1922 or at an even earlier date. I believe hon. members will agree with me when I say that more efficient machinery either for the movement of dirt or for the
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

making of farm implements or machinery of war has not resulted in lesser costs for the completed process or articles. I believe if we check back over the whole list of articles being produced to-day we shall find that the theory that present-day equipment reduces costs has not worked out in actual practice. If we consider the cost of replacing machinery from time to time, it is costing just about as much to move earth to-day as it did back in the days when they were building the railways across western Canada in the first instance. I am not at all carried away with the idea that we can move this dirt to-day at half what it cost a few years go. It still costs a great deal of money to move earth to carry out projects of the type mentioned.
The estimate with regard to the Pearce scheme, made I think in 1922 by the then Department of the Interior, was that it would cost about S54 an acre to irrigate lands in the vicinity of Sullivan Lake. That is the 425,000 acres of which we were speaking a moment ago. It was also estimated that it would cost $78 an acre to irrigate those lands which were located in Saskatchewan. The question which arises in my mind, and in the minds of many others, is whether it is advisable for this government to start to spend sums of that kind in order to develop irrigation projects at this particular time. There may come a time when it will be advisable to do that, but I do not think that time has arrived as yet.
With regard to the suggestion that there may have been discrimination as between Alberta and other provinces in the expenditure of money, I can only say that as far as expenditures upon water conservation are concerned the amount spent in Alberta compares favourably with what was spent in Saskatchewan or Manitoba, that is in proportion to the areas. In connection with regrassing and reseeding lands, and work of that type, the same thing is true. Alberta has had a fair share of the money which has been expended for these different purposes. In 1937 we undertook to enlarge the activities carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and endeavoured to establish community pastures here and there throughout the drought areas or the open prairie country. The advisory committee met on two or three occasions, and finally a resolution was adopted setting out a certain policy for the development of the land reclamation activities to be carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. In line with those activities we have been attempting to take certain lands east of Hanna, somewhat similar to those described a few moments ago by the hon. member, out 
of cultivation and put them back into grass which could be used by farmers who are on better land roundabout.
We were able to enter into negotiations with the government of Saskatchewan by which they agreed to the policies which were then laid down and adopted by the federal Department of Agriculture. We carried on negotiations with the government of Alberta, but they were not prepared to turn over lands in what were known as the special areas in the province and which had been administered by the special areas board since I think about 1922. They were not prepared to turn over those lands to the government on the same terms as lands were being turned over in Saskatchewan. As they desired to carry on activities within those areas themselves, we suggested that we were prepared to enter into agreements under which lands outside that area would be leased to us for twenty-one years. Under these leases we would be prepared to go on and do the same sort of work we were doing in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Tanner, a member of the government of Alberta, came to Ottawa, and a mutual agreement was drawn up which we felt stated the understanding as to what might be done in the areas outside the special areas. Since then, however, we have had no communication from the government of Alberta stating that they were prepared to proceed with the plan. As we were not able to arrive at definite conclusions during the summer of 1937, about $250,000 which had been voted to be expended under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was never taken out of the treasury. In other words, we held the money throughout a whole year while endeavouring to enter into some arrangements with the government of Alberta which would make possible the expenditure of that money. I think any money which was not expended would have to be charged up to Alberta when making a calculation as to what money was available to Alberta in that particular year.

speechtext: I do not know. They have not told me. Since the agreement which was drawn up while Mr. Tanner was in Ottawa, was sent to the Alberta government, I have had no further communication from them.

speechtext:
Is it not true that the advisory committee met in June when it was understood that the administration of these areas would be left in the hands of the provincial government? Then, later on in the year the Saskatchewan government submitted

a different kind of plan which the federal government adopted. Alberta was never allowed to submit its plan. Saskatchewan submitted a plan which the federal government adopted, but the federal government did not permit Alberta to submit a similar plan.

speechtext: The hon. member is speaking of 1936?

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: In 1936, to go back of 1937, negotiations were started early in the spring. The committee was called together and our plans for the work were discussed. Later on the advisory committee met in Regina and discussed a possible program. None of the provinces, however, was prepared to go on with that particular plan. We worked along until about August, but at that time there were no works of the type of which I have been speaking which were ready to be proceeded with. In August the committee was again called together in order to arrive at a working plan, which was laid down, I think on August 2. From there on we proceeded to organize this pasture scheme in Saskatchewan and attempted to organize it in Alberta and Manitoba. We did organize one large pasture in Manitoba to take care of shipments of live stock from the drought areas in the other provinces to the market in Winnipeg and elsewhere late in the season. The other matters of which I have spoken were dealt with partly in 1936 and continued in 1937.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: Was not one of the objections that of turning lands over to the federal government?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
That was in [DOT]connection with the special areas of which I spoke a moment ago. They objected to turning lands in the special areas over to the federal government because they had an organization set up to administer them. We said that we were prepared to go on with the water conservation work, with the building of dams, dug-outs and so on, that we were ready to assist in regrassing lands and helping in every way possible with their own activities. But where lands were turned over to us we would not undertake the moving of settlers or the placing of settlers upon other land. We took the position that if they desired to hold the lands in that province under their own control, then they could see to it that persons were moved from one section of the province to the other on to lands controlled by the province. There had
not been any understanding reached up to that time with regard to the pasture areas either inside the special areas or outside.
There was one special case, in connection with the Bartman dam, where tenders were called for a year ago, and as was stated, the lowest bidder was the special areas board of the provincial government. The second lowest bidder was the Poole Construction Company, with offices at Edmonton and Regina. The position taken by the department at that time was that it was not fair to call for tenders and allow governments to tender against private individuals in connection with any undertaking of the federal government. We had, of course, entered into scores of contracts with the provincial government, but we had not called for tenders. We had passed many projects for dams, community dug-outs and community water conservation projects of different kinds, which were carried through by the special areas board of Alberta, but in those instances we did not call for tenders. We simply give them the work, and they see that it is carried out on a day labour basis by persons living within the community. When we have called for tenders we have not permitted the provincial government to tender. In the particular instance mentioned, that of the Bartman dam, they did tender, but we gave the work to the lowest private bidder, the Poole Construction Company.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: Why was it thought advisable to have this work done by tender?

We are giving a considerable amount of cash money to the province for projects of this kind, and we did not think it was fair in asking for tenders to allow the government to tender against private concerns. It was a case either of not calling for tenders and giving the work to the provincial government or of eliminating governments from making tenders, and that policy has been carried out both in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Mr.'SENN:	Did I understand the minister to say that under this act the federal department pay all the expenditures on these dams?
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

Is there anything paid

this evening has concerned Alberta more particularly. speechtext:
Before leaving the
questions asked by the hon. member for Acadia, there was one other matter, the Medicine Hat irrigation proposal. There is west of Medicine Hat the Canada Land and Irrigation Company's land, where an irrigation project was undertaken many years ago while the lands were still owned, controlled and operated from Ottawa. An agreement was entered into at that time under which a British company was going to settle a considerable area, after having placed water upon the land. Financial difficulties arose, and after the company had spent something in the neighbourhood of $13,000,000 in developing an irrigation project in that area, the company found itself unable to extend its operations. If my memory serves me correctly, the amount of land in that district which was irrigated is in the neighbourhood of 45,000 acres. There are people living on those 45,000 acres, and two or three years ago we spent about $80,000, in assisting these people in obtaining water from the Bow river, some one hundred miles distant. We assisted them by taking care of some of the works which were installed in the earlier years, and which were in a deteriorated condition and would have become useless in a very short time. We had a little difficulty later because a certain community in Alberta desired water from these same ditches and we were not able to make arrangements under which that water could be supplied. We took the position at the time that if we ever again had to deal with the Canadian Land and Irrigation Company we would want an undertaking from them, in connection with the supply of water to others outside the community that they had organized, which would be satisfactory to the government.
A short time ago a delegation from Alberta suggested that we enter into an arrangement which would require an agreement of some kind with this company. The

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
first proposal was that we spend $3,500,000 to assist in widening the ditches that supplied that area, the province of Alberta, this company and ourselves thus making it possible to irrigate other areas of land that would be available for re-settlement. I stated at that time that it was impossible for the government to consider spending $3,500,000, which Was the total vote for this purpose, on this area of 60,000,000 acres of land, in orijer to take care of, at the outside, 2,000 families in the neighbourhood of Medicine Hat; that if that project were ever to be considered it would have to be at some time when many of our other activities had been completed. As a resut of that decision a smaller project was proposed which would involve the turning over of part of the lands of the Canada Land and Irrigation Company to the dominion government for the settlement of persons who were being taken off some of these submarginal lands. That is the proposal which at the moment has not been given final consideration, and I can give no further information concerning it now.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: To what extent has any other province gone in the development of anything corresponding to the special areas board which Alberta has developed? My reason for asking this question is that we feel that as a province we have gone a long way in dealing with a problem which was "wished" upon us; it was not our making, as the minister recognized the other night. The settlement of those areas was carried out by the dominion government without our control. We have spent a great deal of money and gone to a great deal of trouble to develop a special areas board and deal with the problem. If the minister can show us that any other province has gone as far as Alberta has in that matter, it would make us feel a little better.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
I have not gone over the record, so I have not the information before me concerning the special areas board in Alberta. They have done good work in persuading people to move from these areas, but I do not think they have spent any considerable amount of money in doing so. It is now some sixteen years since the activities were started, and the only year I can recall is the last year before we began to assist them. I think the total expenditure that year was about $16,000. What it was in preceding years I am not prepared to say, but they were not spending any considerable amount of money in the last year or two before we joined in the activities, I suppose largely on account of the
difficult conditions existing under which they could not obtain money. I do not suppose the federal government would ever have come into the picture in any of the western provinces had it not been for the great difficulty of the years following 1931 and 1932. It was those difficulties that caused the federal government to undertake some activities in that area.
I may say in direct answer to the question oi the hon. member I do not know that any other province spent any considerable sums in doing the same thing. The province of Saskatchewan spent considerable sums in 1920, 1921, and 1922, the year that Alberta began to encourage people to move away from that area, in moving people out of the section immediately north of Maple Creek, which is just across the boundary line from these special areas, and also moving people from farther north into far north country; but after a few years, when moisture was again falling on those lands, they found that many of those people came back and re-settled on the land they had left. That is, from 1922 on people returned, and my memory is that a very' large percentage, I think well over half, of the people, some of whom were assisted, and some of whom went of their own free will from that area, came back and re-settled there. With that experience in mind it has been the desire of the department and the government to take on this occasion action which will make it unlikely that people will come back and re-settle on these lands, because we know that if they do so it will result in greater and greater expenditures of money over the years in providing relief and that kind of thing which we have had to do in the last few years.
So, while I do not know that any other government has taken the same course as Alberta, and I do not think any other government did set up a board and attempt to operate in that way, the government of Saskatchewan passed legislation, which I think they term the Reclamation Act, and they have a special arrangement with the municipal bodies in that province under which the municipal bodies take over land by tax sale and otherwise to be kept out of cultivation. Those lands are turned over to us free of charges, and our reason for asking that the provincial government turn these lands over to us is in order that they may be kept out of cultivation when we have once spent money in order to get them out of cultivation. We think those lands should then be placed under the control of the body that spent the money, and put in a position where it is not likely that they will come back into cultivation.
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

It is for that reason that we are rather anxious to have the other provinces enter into some agreement.

speechtext: In June, 1936, an agreement was arrived at whereby these community pastures would be fenced by the federal government and left under the administration of the provincial government. But the Alberta government had agreed to abide by the original arrangement and were willing to go ahead with it. Then the federal government turned round and told Alberta it would have to acpept the same agreement as Saskatchewan. I do not think that was fair; the Alberta government were quite prepared to go ahead under the original agreement reached in June, 1936; but just because Saskatchewan submitted another agreement which was more acceptable to the federal government, the latter turned round and presented an ultimatum to Alberta requiring them to accept a new agreement.

I am just looking up

find it impossible to get anywhere? Alberta was all prepared; they had the land all ready and had started to move the settlers.

The main reason it
was impossible to get anywhere was that the arrangement made at that time was to the effect that the mortgage companies, the railway companies, the Hudson's Bay Company and the land companies generally represented on that committee were quite willing to turn over lands on certain conditions to be put into pastures which were to be fenced by the federal government, but we found that there was great difficulty in the provinces dealing with the persons who owned

the land when they did not have the money to deal with them, and get the lands evacuated to be put into pasture.

speechtext:
Is it not a fact that
Alberta had already acquired the lands by tax sale?

speechtext:
No; there is one area
that Alberta wants to deal with on which there are two or three hundred families. But there are many areas that have not been cleared at all. Some of those that have been cleared by tax sale, to the extent that the individual has gone, have not yet been placed in a position where any one else can claim title to them, and immediately the government comes along with a sum of money, the hon. member for Acadia will agree that there are always individuals who come back into the picture with some idea that they can collect. Our difficulty was this-and it did not make any difference what province we were in-that sometimes a dozen or more individuals would not enter into the agreement until they actually saw the money. The province would get options from them, discuss the matter with them and would then come back to the federal government and declare that they were ready to deal with these people if the federal government could supply them with the money; but by the time we got into a position to supply the money the individual had raised the' price or had taken some other attitude which we were not prepared to meet, with the result that \ve were not getting anywhere with the activities of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in relation to these projects.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: There are some large areas that have been completely taken over for taxes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but some of these are not of that nature where you would want to have a . community pasture, and the Alberta government are not desirous of having a community pasture in such places. The plan followed is to allow certain 'families to use the surrounding lands for live stock purposes. Y ith that condition prevailing, by August we came to the conclusion that we would not get anywhere in trying to carry out the plans we had under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act unless, when the time came for negotiation, we could associate ourselves directly with the persons concerned. So that the operating arrangement now made is for the province to evacuate all the land they can by tax sale. They obtain any understandings they can with companies and individuals and then make a proposal to us:

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
and if they have sufficiently eliminated difficulties from their proposal to make it possible for it to be carried out, then we undertake to proceed further, to negotiate directly with the individuals and to make whatever arrangements are necessary to get the whole project cleared up and under way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not my wish to interrupt this unusually friendly discussion between the minister and hon. members from Alberta, but I should like to make one or two observations. Listening to the great problem of resettling our friends in western Canada who have suffered from drought conditions,
I have been thinking that we in Manitoba have not suffered to anything like the same extent; in fact, there are in Manitoba areas that have not suffered at all from crop failure.
I heard the minister say that this project will cost so many hundreds of thousands of dollars, and I believe I heard the sum of $3,500,000 mentioned to-night. I cannot help thinking that we might save a good deal of this expenditure and still not interfere too much with nature. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
There is something very much different between the interlake country in Manitoba and the country we are discussing. One difference is that they have a more
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

bountiful rainfall. The prairie farm rehabilitation moneys are not for expenditure upon lands where the rainfall is sufficient. If we were to undertake that sort of work probably we should have to extend our operations from one end of Canada to the other. The activities under this measure are in relation to lands where the rainfall is comparatively light.
It is hardly correct to say that all lands being fenced into pastures are like the lands referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Acadia. For example, there is an area in the southern end of Saskatchewan where buffalo grass grows naturally. There is all the difference in the world between buffalo grass and the grass up between the two lakes in Manitoba. Buffalo grass, in the short grass country, will finish cattle. They do not require any grain; they are finished on the grass, and even short grass in that country is very much more valuable as feed than long grass in some other areas.
In addition to that, may I say that while in 1937 that part of the country looked like summer fallow, though it had never been broken up, in 1938 one could cut the grass on that same land with a binder. I make that statement in order to indicate to hon. members that in a country of that kind there are possibilities that have to be dealt with having regard to the surrounding conditions. What we are attempting in that area is to take that large pasture I just mentioned, which contains 130,000 acres and which was almost bare in 1937, not out of cultivation because it never was cultivated, but out of ranching. It was pastured down in the dry years so as to be almost useless even for ranching purposes. We are making of it what we call a reserve pasture. We will never permit anyone to settle on it; we will never permit it to be leased again for ranching purposes. We will maintain it as open prairie country upon which we can run live stock in years when we have difficulties in regard to feed, thus removing the necessity of shipping cattle to the central part of Manitoba or bringing seed all the way from Three Rivers in Quebec. That is our objective in connection with a pasture of that kind. The people are not going to move out of that country; the land is too good. When it does rain there they get good crops, and even if they have to go for three or four years without crops they are going to continue to live there in the hope that they may get three or four of those bountiful crops to which they have been accustomed in the past. We think it is very

much better for the government so to organize that country that they can stay there and make a living without being government charges during years when they are without rain.
