These pastures are
organized in this way. First, the municipality approaches the provincial government and asks to have a certain area organized into a pasture. The provincial government undertakes to have the lands evacuated by any persons who are living within the area. They usually succeed up to a point where only one or two are left. We then investigate the pasture to see whether it is possible to get those people who remain moved out on to lands immediately adjacent. We then put a

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
fence round the lands and make them available to the people who are living roundabout. They pay a fee for putting their live stock into the pasture, and these fees are supposed to cover all costs of maintenance including the maintaining of the fences and the paying of the pasture manager. We assist as a government in raising the standard of the live stock within that pasture.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: The government inspector decides how many cattle the pasture will carry. The grass is investigated by a man having the technical skill necessary to determine how many cattle or how many cattle and horses can be carried. We then take in the farmers in the first mile round the pasture, then those in the second mile, and so on until we get a sufficient number of farmers having approximately two-thirds of the stock the pasture will carry. The farmers are then asked to form themselves into a community pasture association and appoint a committee to operate the pasture. We allow' them to divide up the acreage and determine how much live stock in relation to the acreage shall be put in. We set up certain regulations which apply to the pasture. Hon. members may want to know the reason for placing the limit at two-thirds. In all probability after these men have gained a little experience they will want to add to their own herds or admit other farmers to the pasture. We leave it to them to determine what shall be done within certain limits, but we do not permit them to put in more cattle than the lands will properly carry.

We are not jealous of the prairie provinces, but we do not want them to pull the blanket too much to their side. There are good people in the province of Quebec; there are good people in the province of Ontario, there are good people in the maritime provinces, and we want our share. The farmers in some parts of Quebec are in distress. I live in one of the finest constituencies in Canada, but there have been forest fires in my constituency and there are settlers who are almost starving. Irrigation is sorely needed, and I should like this policy to be applied to Temiseouata constituency just the same as it is applied to the three prairie provinces. The western people are our brothers. We are good Samaritans and are ready to give them help, but on the other hand we do not think we should unclothe ourselves for them. The farmers and settlers in my constituency are in distress, and I want them to have at least as much as their western brothers.

I thank my hon. friend for saying that. He knows my request is fair.
For the enlightenment of members of the committee I should like to describe a most absurd division of land which was made some years ago in my constituency by the provincial government. In order to make this distribution they used maps which contained no elevations. There were no hills and valleys, and the lands were divided like pieces of cake without taking into consideration the ups and downs of the country. Some of the settlers at St. Jean de la Lande parish, which the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) knows very well, have been placed on the side of a * steep hill and are apparently supposed to cultivate rocks. It is no easier to cultivate rocks than it is to try to cultivate under drought conditions. These men were induced to go there by former immigration agents who were employees of the railway company. They were well paid and in order to justify their positions they had to attempt to show that a
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

conquest was being made of the soil. These settlers are just like the goats on the side of a mountain.
Many of these people are suffering. I have received many letters, some of which I sent to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), some to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and some to other members of the cabinet. When one of these men is very ill and is sent to the hospital for an operation, his family cannot get relief. I have had to write letters in order that a family might be given enough to subsist while a father or mother was in the hospital for an operation. These people are suffering and they need help. The government has done something for our western brothers, and I want something to be done for the settlers and farmers of Temiscouata constituency. We have suffered from the cutting of trees on a very large scale; there have also been forest fires at times, and by reason of the disappearance of timber, irrigation is badly needed to keep a certain amount of moisture in the soil in order that we may not have poor crops, one every second year or one every three years. We need crops regularly, a good average crop.
In many old parishes in my constituency there are good, sound, progressive farmers who have suffered from the drought, although perhaps not so much so as farmers in certain sections of the west, but they have suffered from the drought nevertheless, because of the trees having been cut. Hon. members are familiar with the comparsion between the straw roof and the tin roof. On a tin roof the water runs away fast, but a straw roof holds the water from running away fast. The water runs off a straw roof little by little, and it is the same with the land. The trees are a protection and hold the moisture longer in the land.
I want a fair and square deal for the farmers and settlers of Temiscouata constituency and of the province of Quebec at large. What would happen if we all died of hunger in the east? It would then be for the west to support us, and the western provinces would be very much embarrassed to do for us what we do for them. They should keep that in mind when they come here making requests, and when they make a request they should be fair enough to cut their request in two and let us have fifty per cent for necessary works in the east. We would be satisfied with that fifty per cent. I want to tell that to my hon. friends from the west.
I should also like to say to the Minister of Agriculture, who has been powerful enough to succeed in having the government change its policy, that I hope he will not forget the

eastern provinces. I remember that complaints were made against the Minister of Labour for not receiving the mayor and council of Toronto. He would not deal with any city because it was outside the constitution for him to do so. The constitution has not been amended since; it is still the same constitution, and yet the Minister of Agriculture can deal directly with the municipalities, although the Minister of Labour Says that he cannot. I should like a policy that is uniform, and when one member of the cabinet can deal with municipalities I should like his colleagues to have the same power. I wonder if it is really within the constitution or outside the constitution. I would not recommend anything unconstitutional, but when a thing is done for one part of the country it should be constitutional to do it for the whole country. That is my humble understanding.
May I place on record what I want. In the fiist place I want the lake Morin dam developed at Riviere du Loup. I did not have the opportunity to discuss it with the minister, but the Minister of Labour is thoroughly familiar with the project, as are the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), and I do not not know whether I have not spoken to my chief about it also. That is one thing, and a very important thing, because the city of Riviere du Loup has her own municipal plant, dating back to long before the time of Sir Adam Beck. Moreover, the dam would serve other purposes-

speechtext:

minister has entered directly into contacts with municipalities and individuals as mentioned by the hon. member for Temiseouata?

speechtext: There are undertakings on the part of municipalities to operate some of the pastures, and there are undertakings on the part of individuals in some instances. We hire men to do the work, just the same as we hire anyone else to do other work.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: Are contracts entered into directly by the government with the municipalities?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes; arrangements are
made by the government with municipalities all over Canada to do many things. We shall probably have some undertakings in connection with many of the cities and towns of the province of Quebec this year, as we always have had in connection with works carried on there.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: How many of these individual associations have been formed to deal with these large areas?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: When this land is being turned over from the provinces to the dominion under this plan, who retains the mineral rights on that land-the province or the dominion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The province simply
turns over to the government the right to operate the land as a pasture; we get the land the same as a person purchasing it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: Does the province retain the mineral rights?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
We would have no
objection to that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister was explaining
how these different associations were set up, who determines the number of cattle that could be placed on a pasture by each member of the association, and how the amount of fees paid for each head of cattle was determined. I should like to have him finish that explanation, because I was under the

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

impression that the fees are not very large, perhaps only large enough to pay the actual running expenses of the pasture; so it seemed to me that farmers were getting very cheap pasture, and it might pay them better to have cattle pastured in these government pastures than to keep them on their own places.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The pastures are more
or less tributary to a man's farm; they are community pastures in the same sense as the common land in the older countries. The pasture equipment is not only fences but corrals and everything necessary for the proper keeping of several hundred head of cattle. The breeding sires are put in the pasture under the care of the manager of the pasture, and the whole breeding policy of that area is under his direction. The fees are made sufficient to cover not only the payment of the manager and the cost of other services, but to take care of maintenance and repairs to fencing and buildings and that kind of thing. In the first year the fees collected were slightly under the amount expended for those purposes-I have not the exact figure-and it will take two or three years of running experience to know exactly what the fees should be. But it is intended that the fees shall as nearly as possible cover the actual outlay. The whole policy and intent are to enable the farmers living in the surrounding sub-marginal lands, lands not of the highest type, to run live stock on these pasture lands which could not be occupied successively by individuals, and by having the right to run stock on those lands the farmers on adjoining lands should be able to maintain themselves and keep off relief. The intention is to do exactly what has been suggested by the hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Senn), that is to make it less costly for the individual to maintain himself because of this common land being there.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: I was not finding any particular fault with the plan except that there might be one or two members of that association who own a large number of cattle, and naturally they will get more advantage from the land than a man who may be just as needy but has not so many cattle. Some provision whereby one or two or a few farmers may not monopolize the whole pasture seems to me desirable.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
That is taken care of in the regulations and the set-up of the committee. In the first place we do not form pastures for ranchers. These pastures are formed for people who are farming from a

half section to a section of land in the neighbourhood of the pasture. They may have ten or twenty or thirty cattle each. They themselves take care of the matter referred to; they see that no one has too large a number of cattle. We also have regulations which govern them in that respect.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: Do the regulations provide that cattle of the same breed shall be kept in the community pastures?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: The intention is to confine the breeds more or less to the three chief beef varieties, the Black Angus, the Shorthorn and the Hereford. That will be controlled by the association; they will determine which breed they desire to have, and all in the association will have to have the same breed, or breeds of the same type.

speechtext: In connection with the thirty odd community pastures involving nearly one thousand miles of fencing, how were the posts and wire secured? Did they get any of the posts in the northern part of Saskatchewan, or were they brought from British Columbia?

speechtext: Have they a contract with the Northern Wood Preserving Company of Prince Albert for getting out posts, and how many posts did they get from that company?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The Northern Wood Preserving Company has just established a plant in Prince Albert this last year. Prior to this time our posts were obtained largely from British Columbia; we had to ship cedar posts all the way from British Columbia, and have them tarred before they were put in the ground. Last year we tried to get some posts in the northern part of Saskatchewan and blue-stoned them. We have carried on experiments at the Swift Current farm which indicate that blue-stoned poplar posts will last about twenty years and give good service. We obtained blue-stone posts last year from the northern part of the province for a considerable portion of our supplies. I do not know exactly the percentage, but in the pastures spoken of in some of the eastern papers recently, the one in the southwestern part of the province, it was said to have been built with rough posts simply taken out of the bluffs here and there. In the first place, I would point out that there are no bluffs to take posts out of; and every second post was said to be a cedar post brought from British Columbia and tarred to the ground. Every second post was a blue-stone poplar post shipped from the northern end of Saskatchewan for fencing.
Again, the fence was not a three-wire fence, but a four-wire fence. The farmers there do not usually build a four-wire fence. So that this fence was of a higher cost of construction. The farmers in that area usually go to the Cypress hills, cut their own pickets, take them down and do their fencing there, but this fence was built with posts shipped in, because we do not want to have to replace them every four or five years. We want to have these pasture fences remain at least during the lifetime of the leases. We have leased some of the lands for twenty or twenty-five years, and the fences we put up to-day will probably stand for fifty years. The Northern Wood Preserving Company put in a plant last year at Prince Albert, and they can creosote jack pine and poplar posts in -that establishment. We have given them a contract to supply
400,000	posts next summer. No posts have been supplied from that plant to date. They are being supplied for the work next summer; we expect to get them at a very much lower 71492-1311	'
cost than those we have had shipped in from long distances, and at the same time employment will be provided for people in the vicinity.

The people in that vicinity are particularly concerned because these dams higher up in the river have cut off their normal water supply, and they are anxious that something should be done to get more water down the river to fill up their own water-holes and give them a normal flow of water, or that their water supply be protected in some other way. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
If we get our estimates through the house we are proposing to spend this year $500 for the purpose of carrying on further investigational work in connection with a dam at Wawanesa. The Souris river has its source in the province of Saskatchewan; then it runs into the state of North Dakota and then comes back into Manitoba. As a result there is some difficulty between the two provinces and the state of North Dakota on account of the fact that there has never been an international agreement in connection with the -Souris river. Most of the streams, such as the Milk river, which is further west, and Frenchman's river, are covered by international agreements, but none has been negotiated with regard to the Souris river. There is sufficient storage capacity in the loop in the United States to take up all the water that flows into North Dakota from Saskatchewan. In other words, if our United States friends so desired, and an arrangement were not entered into, they could keep all the water that accumulates in the province of Saskatchewan and flows into the United States.
At the present time negotiations are under way, through the international joint commission, looking to an agreement between the United States and Canada in regard to the Souris river. I do not anticipate that there will be any great difficulty, since there has been none in the past. The two countries have been quite reasonable about these matters, and in all probability that will be the case in this instance, but at the moment the matter is in the negotiation stage.

speechtext:
Did the minister give
us the details in connection with the Goven-lock pasture? I did not hear them if he did. Could I have the details?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I had not reached the Govenlock pasture when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle thought he would not like any more of the list read. In our list this is known as the Nashlyn grazing area, special area A. It has fifty-seven miles of fencing; its acreage is 62,240, and the entire cost of construction was $28,237.59, which is considerably less than fifty cents an acre for the setting up of the pasture. This is the pasture to which I was referring a few moments ago when I said the fence was not a three-wire but a four-wire fence and when I said the posts were not pickets but cedar posts tarred up to the top of the ground, alternately with poplar posts that have been blue-stoned and thus made so that, according to our experience, they will last for at least twenty years.
In regard to an article which appeared in an eastern paper recently, I might just say that no barbed wire has been left lying round the place; it has been all rolled up and put away. Any barbed wire which was not used was wire which it would not pay anyone to use in building a new fence. If you have what is known as black barbed wire, not galvanized, that has been in a fence for some time, of course that wire will not stand stretching on a new fence, but it can be used in the cross-fencing of the pasture, and in this case any of this wire available will be so used ultimately. The outside fences have to be sufficiently strong to keep the stock which is put in by the farmers from getting out and damaging the crops. Again, anyone who has handled barbed wire knows that if you take it off a fence and allow it to lie round loose it kinks up, and when you start to stretch that wire with the kinks in it the wire ultimately breaks, if not while you are stretching it, then perhaps the first day after you leave it. In putting up a fence of this kind round an area containing 62,640 acres, we have not taken any chances by using wire of that kind. The cost of maintenance and of riding the fence would be so great, if we undertook to do anything of that kind, that the ultimate cost would be very much higher than the cost of using new wire in the first place and using the older wire for crossfencing. That cross-fencing has not been done as yet, but the wire is available.

speechtext:
Before saying what I had in mind, may I commend the minister, as I have done on several occasions, for his interest and consistent work in developing the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. But in the light of what has been said to-night I feel, there are one or two observations which really ought to be made, so as to keep us all working together in Canada as a big family.
There are points of view in the west which probably easterners would not understand, unless they were given reasons. For a few moments I should like to set forth some of those points. The minister seemed to have the idea that the provinces could not be trusted to keep the land from being settled again, after the dominion had developed pastures. I would say, in passing, that the main difference between Alberta and the dominion over matters connected with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act seems to be that the province does not feel it ought to give up control of its lands simply because the dominion develops under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I believe the reason for that difference needs to be set forth.
From what the minister said a few minutes ago I gathered he had a sort of apprehension that if the provinces had control of those lands they would be tempted to allow people to go back in upon them to settle, whereas if the dominion had control there would be less danger of that unfortunate occurrence. Was that the minister's idea?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The idea was not that the province could not be trusted to do it. The position is that the province has no money with which to carry out these operations at the present time-at least the provinces .say they have not. All three provinces make that statement.
Before the present government took office the federal authorities undertook to carry on activities for the rehabilitation of that area. Since the present government has taken office we have [DOT] carried on and enlarged upon the activities established by the previous government. But we have felt that since we are putting up the money, and the money is given to us in trust by the taxpayers of Canada to reestablish that country-and it is not a matter of not trusting the province-having spent the money of the people of Canada it is our obligation to take the people off that land, to reestablish the country and to see that the policy is carried out.
While we might trust the government of Alberta to do just exactly what we might expect them to do, we do not know, of course, what government is going to be in Alberta
(Mr. Gardiner.]
or in any other province in the future. For that reason we feel that if anyone is going to undo the work it should be the government which spent the money in the first place-not necessarily the government in office at the moment, but the government which represents all the people of Canada and which collected money from all the taxpayers of Canada in order that it should carry on the work. We feel that the government representing all the people should accept the obligation of either keeping that land out of cultivation or in the future putting it back into cultivation. So far as the present government is concerned, we think it should never go back into cultivation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad the minister has made that point clear, because I must say I did get the wrong impression from what he said earlier. I was going to make several observations which, under the present circumstances, I do not now propose to make.
With respect to the matter the minister has recently laid before us, may I say it is well that the people of Canada should understand that the west has a very real case which makes them feel, when they get their eyes thoroughly opened, that there is another side to what the minister has just said.
In the first place it was developed last year by an eminent authority in Ottawa that the three prairie provinces have, through tariffs, paid in the neighbourhood of S47,000,000 a year into the dominion treasury. That has been going on for a long time. The result is that when $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 are set aside for expenditures in connection with a proposition like prairie farm rehabilitation, we are likely to think of that $47,000,000 instead of the $3,000,000. After all is said and done, that is a matter which ought to be borne constantly in mind. I am sure the minister, coming from the west, will appreciate that point of view.
The remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata show the importance of keeping these facts before our minds. In the west we are paying a large amount of money through the tariff. We are not getting any direct return from that expenditure, as are the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We are not wishing to complain, but we do want hon. members to see our point of view. For a few moments may I indicate to hon. members some of the disadvantages from which we have suffered, and about which the hon. member for Temiscouata would no doubt like to hear. These are disadvantages which we have not been able to avoid.
The land settlement policies which for years were followed by dominion governments, and

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
which on one or two occasions have been referred to in the house, have placed the three prairie provinces, and particularly Alberta and Saskatchewan, under a handicap which I believe is hardly realized by the rest of the dominion. In order to appreciate the situation we should remember that at least two great projects were paid for with land. One of these was the Hudson's Bay Company project. When the Hudson's Bay Company were persuaded to give up their holdings in the west they were allowed one-twentieth of the land surveyed in the townships from the United States boundary to the North Saskatchewan. One-twentieth was taken out here, there and all over the prairie provinces, and, in most instances, out of the choicest lands. When the time came for settlement people had to settle all round those pieces of land. This meant that the population was widely scattered. The extent to which Alberta alone is suffering to-day from that situation is remarkable. Before concluding my observations on this subject I shall say one or two things to indicate the extent of that suffering.
When the Canadian Pacific railway was built, the company were promised 25,000,000 acres, with mineral rights. According to figures I have they received about 18,000,000 acres. All hon. members have to do is to think of the colossal extent of 18,000,000 acres, and to remember that this land was selected all over the country and, to a large extent, from the choicest areas, to realize how settlement in the western provinces was spread out.
We say: What bearing has that on the situation? It has a tremendous bearing, and we will see shortly why. In addition, the Canadian Pacific Railway acquired perpetual exemption from taxation on their main line properties and on mineral rights for twenty years. The effect on the western provinces and on the communities in those provinces was serious. It put them under the handicap which started them to go into debt. Fifty-five million acres of prairie land were pledged to one organization or another. Even some other railway projects were supported with land. Unfortunately that land was given largely by Alberta and Saskatchewan. It is estimated that Alberta alone gave 13,120,000 acres. The whole cost, or practically all of it, fell on Alberta and Saskatchewan. Those provinces paid for not only -the railroad in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, -but for the railroad in western Ontario and British Columbia. I think this is a matter which should be kept steadily in mind -by hon. members.
I will say that since I have come down here I have found hon. members disposed to be
very sympathetic to the west, which is entirely as it ought to be, but we should still like to be understood a little more. I notice to-night that certain statements have been made -that since we are asking for certain things, we should be willing to divide up. All we are asking for is the right to live. But we find ourselves placed in a position where it is impossible to carry on. The impossibility of our situation has been developed through the years by conditions like the one I have just mentioned. This spreading out of our settlement has affected our economy. I can jump right into the middle just as well as I can start at the beginning, but I rather like to start at the beginning. The minister has raised the question of the province not being able to pay any money. The province cannot pay any money for the development of these projects on lands which the dominion government's policy allowed to be settled entirely without the say of -the province. The minister pointed this out as the reason why the dominion should control the administration of the lands in question. I think it is quite clear now how this has a bearing on the subject. There are large areas in Alberta and Saskatchewan which were wished upon those provinces right over their heads. They are grappling with these situations. They have been placed under handicaps which are manifestly unjust and unfair. The dominion says that they will come in to help, but the provinces must give up the land. Just as soon as we got control of our lands we began to look after them. We did not obtain control of our lands until 1930, but immediately we did so we made stipulations which prevented the settlement of the country in such a way as to put us under a handicap. Having said that, I shall go on to say what I was going to say a minute ago. Because of the spreading out of our settlement Alberta has had to pay twenty per cent more for its telephone service than is

paid in Ontario. For highways it costs us 500 per cent more per thousand than it does in Ontario.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OP OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: When the dominion allowed the Canadian Pacific and the Hudson's Bay Company to select large areas of the choicest land, settlers coming in were forced to go on sub-marginal lands. The province of Alberta then had to undertake to keep those people on those lands. The province now finds it necessary to get help in taking care of those people. They feel they should have this as a just right. There is the connection of the whole thing with the question under discussion. I shall say no more about it because I have gone far enough to indicate that this matter is all bound up in our thinking. The province of Alberta is under a tremendous burden, but there is no province in the dominion to-day that is making a more determined effort to manage its affairs and its economy. We know what we are doing, but many people do not know. They say silly and unjustifiable things, but they do not convince us. We know, we are right there.

I hope no hon.
member asks me a question which I shall have to answer. I am going to say this again. We feel that money should be spent in Alberta as far as these lands are concerned. When these lands are rehabilitated, the men who go on them will be buying commodities upon which duty will be paid; they will be buying goods upon which the sales tax will be paid, and both the duty and the 
sales tax will go directly into the dominion treasury. The result is that the dominion is bound to get as much value out of these settlers as is any province. Why should the dominion hesitate to spend money to prepare the lands so that people can live there? We do not want to be stubborn or uncooperative. I think the minister will bear me out when I say that, generally speaking, the ministers from Alberta have been as cooperative as any group of ministers from anjr other province in the dominion. There are certain things to which they hold steadily, and this is one. They feel and we feel that if in the future there are obligations which result from the fact that the dominion owns certain lands in a province and the province has responsibilities in connection with those lands, then there will be discord which will be altogether undesirable. We would much rather keep control within the province. That is not saying that the dominion should not c.ome in and spend money in the province.
After all, provincial lands are dominion lands just as well as they are provincial lands. The situation cannot possibly be otherwise. I just want to lay that down for the committee so that hon. members can see our point of view. We feel that there should not be any halting because of this requirement that the dominion should have control of provincial lands. I have not the details before me because I have been working along other lines, but there is a tendency on the part of the dominion to take control of land where water is put on by irrigation works. We feel that is not necessary. We feel the dominion should leave control of the lands with the province. After all, the province must provide the schools; it must provide the health and other services which are distinctly provincial. All of these things cost money.

I pointed out the other
evening the extraordinary character of the last of these three subsections, and without labouring the point I am going to make a suggestion to the minister and offer one or two reasons in support of it.
In the first place it is obvious that we are clear away from the emergency character of the original legislation. I think the minister will agree with that because to-night he has indicated that many thousands of acres of land, hundreds of thousands of acres, I think I am safe in saying, have been acquired in

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

the name of the dominion and fenced; and, to use his own language, these fences are being constructed to last at least twenty years. Now there is a definite, permanent work.
Going through the report that was tabled, I find in harmony with what the minister has been saying to-night a lengthy recital of most important projects of one kind and another. Therefore this is no longer emergency legislation. Let us get that clear in our minds.
I am going to suggest to the minister that section 2 be amended in this way. I suggest that these three subsections be eliminated and that instead we have paragraphs A, B and C; and A would read, "The minister may, for the purpose of this act, and subject to section four, and with the approval of the governor in council, enter into agreements," and so forth.
Then, instead of having subsection 11, put in B, leaving out the words "The minister may, for the purposes of the act," because that would be repetition, and saying, "B. Purchase, lease or otherwise acquire," and so forth.
Then when you come to the next subsection 12, eliminate the first line and make it read, "C. Purchase or rent whatever machinery," and so forth.
This simply means that the powers granted here will be subject to the act, subject to section 4, and subject also to the approval of the governor in council. It will put all of these powers in the third subsection on exactly the same basis, and I submit that this would improve the legislation. The exact re-drafting would have to be attended to, but I think I have outlined my suggestion with sufficient clarity for the minister to see its importance.

I see no difficulty at all in connection with clauses 10 and 11. The meaning is exactly the same. The only difficulty perhaps would be with clause 12, and I think we could have a re-drafting that probably would serve our purpose just as well and probably avoid some of the reasons for criticism that were made the other night.
The committee will understand that in carrying out one of these irrigation projects requiring an expenditure of some $50,000 or $60,000, when the work is completed you have some machinery partly worn out on which the freight to the next job, which may be one hundred miles away, would be considerable, whereas the machinery can be disposed of on the ground because it is going to be required there for further work. To go through all the process of getting an order in council when you are clearing that up, and

the consequent delays, might make the best and most profitable disposition of that limited amount of property impossible. We want to have some way of dealing with the matter that would be workable.

If the minister will permit a further suggestion, we have, as a regular process in government circles of dealing with just this sort of thing, the salvage department. The minister will not take amiss what I am going to say. Let us just take his illustration. Here is an irrigation project finished up; there are a couple of tractors, maybe a truck or two, power scrapers and so on. Many of these projects run into large sums of money, $70,000, $80,000, $100,000 or more; they are quite substantial works. That machinery is valuable:	If the matter were
wide open, there would be a temptation to let some of that machinery go locally at sacrifice prices. We have the salvage branch, and the governor in council has power under the original act to make regulations. It keeps the wrhole thing working in an orderly way in harmony with good practice in government circles. If that course is departed from, whether by the present minister or future ministers, they are going to be clothed with an authority which I do not think exists in any other .department, or if it does it should not. It is bad legislation, and I say that not in any criticism of the present minister. I urge him to accept the suggestion I made.

I have not any particular objection, but I might point out what it really means. I am now asking this committee, which is composed of the elected representatives of the people, for permission to do this particular thing, sell certain odds and ends that are around, as a departmental matter. The practice in all departments of government is and always has been under every government that items costing up to $5,000 do not go to council, they are dealt with by the minister. This is following the same practice. To follow the suggestion of the hon. member would simply mean that instead of getting permission of this committee of the house, I go to this advisory committee that I picked myself which meets in Regina, and ask them to give me permission to sell this equipment. Knowing they are all business men representing institutions like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the mortgage companies and the banks, men who are used to this kind of thing, I know I shall only have to make the suggestion to get the permission. But instead of asking them for that permission I ask this house, and I think it is much better that I should get permission from the elected representatives of the people than from that group of men whom I really appointed.
